content: Helen Keller, whose full name was Helen Adams Keller, was born on June 27, 1880, in Tuscumbia, Alabama, and passed away on June 1, 1968. She was an American author, activist, and lecturer, and she holds the distinction of being the first deafblind person to graduate from college. Her remarkable journey of overcoming the barriers of deafblindness, with the help of her teacher Anne Sullivan, became widely known through the play The Miracle Worker. This play dramatized how Sullivan broke through Keller's isolation caused by her lack of language, enabling her to communicate and thrive. Keller's early life was marked by a severe illness at 19 months old, described by doctors as acute congestion of the stomach and the brain, which likely was either scarlet fever or meningitis. This illness left her both deaf and blind. Despite these challenges, she developed a rudimentary form of communication with Martha Washington, the young daughter of the family cook, using over 60 home signs by the age of seven. Soviet psychologist Meshcheryakov later emphasized the importance of this early interaction in Keller's psychological development. In 1886, inspired by the story of another deafblind child, Laura Bridgman, Keller's mother sought help from Dr. J. Julian Chisolm, an eye, ear, nose, and throat specialist in Baltimore. This led to a connection with Alexander Graham Bell, who was working with deaf children at the time. Bell recommended contacting the Perkins Institute for the Blind, where Anne Sullivan was trained. Sullivan became Keller's teacher and lifelong companion, beginning a 49-year relationship. Sullivan's first task was to instill discipline in Keller, who had been spoiled due to her disabilities. Keller's breakthrough in communication occurred when she realized that the motions Sullivan made on her palm while water ran over her hand symbolized the word water. This epiphany led to her demanding the names of all objects around her. At the age of ten, Keller was inspired by the story of Ragnhild Kåta, a deafblind Norwegian girl who had learned to speak. Keller was determined to do the same. Sullivan taught her to speak using the Tadoma method, which involved feeling the lips and throat of others as they spoke, combined with fingerspelling letters into her palm. Keller later learned Braille and used it to read in multiple languages, including English, French, German, Greek, and Latin. Keller pursued formal education, attending the Royal Institute for the Blind in 1888 and later the Wright-Humason School for the Deaf and the Horace Mann School for the Deaf in New York City. In 1900, she entered Radcliffe College, supported financially by Standard Oil magnate Henry Huttleston Rogers and his wife, who were introduced to her by Mark Twain. Keller graduated magna cum laude in 1904, becoming the first deafblind person to earn a Bachelor of Arts degree. Anne Sullivan remained Keller's companion even after teaching her. Sullivan married John Macy in 1905, but her health began to decline around 1914. Polly Thompson, a young Scottish woman with no prior experience with deaf or blind individuals, was hired to assist and eventually became Keller's constant companion after Sullivan's death in 1936. Keller and Thompson traveled extensively, raising funds for the blind. After Thompson's death in 1960, Winnie Corbally became Keller's companion for the remainder of her life. Keller was a prolific writer and a world-renowned speaker. She was a staunch advocate for people with disabilities and supported numerous progressive causes, including women's suffrage, workers' rights, socialism, and pacifism. She co-founded the Helen Keller International organization in 1915, focusing on vision, health, and nutrition research, and helped establish the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) in 1920. Keller was a member of the Socialist Party and actively campaigned for workers' rights, supporting Socialist Party candidate Eugene V. Debs in his presidential campaigns. Her political views, however, led to criticism, with some attributing her opinions to her disabilities. Keller's literary contributions include her autobiography The Story of My Life (1903), written during her college years with the help of Sullivan and John Macy. She also authored The World I Live In (1908), which provided insights into her perceptions of the world, and Out of the Dark (1913), a series of essays on socialism. Her spiritual autobiography, My Religion (1927), later reissued as Light in My Darkness, reflected her belief in the teachings of Emanuel Swedenborg. Keller's influence extended beyond her activism and writing. During a visit to Japan in 1937, she expressed interest in the Akita dog breed and was gifted two Akitas, Kamikaze-go and Kenzan-go, introducing the breed to the United States. In her later years, Keller suffered a series of strokes and spent her final years at her home in Connecticut. She was awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 1964 and was inducted into the Women's Hall of Fame in 1965. Keller passed away in her sleep on June 1, 1968, at the age of 87. Her ashes were interred at the National Cathedral in Washington, D.C., alongside those of Anne Sullivan and Polly Thompson. Posthumously, Keller has been honored in various ways, including being listed among Gallup's Most Widely Admired People of the 20th Century in 1999 and being featured on Alabama's state quarter in 2003. Her life has been depicted in numerous films, plays, and documentaries, most notably The Miracle Worker, which dramatized her early life and relationship with Sullivan. However, many portrayals have overlooked her later activism and political views.
